header:
Lithiation Reactions
From the late 30s of the 20th century to the early 50s, Gilmann and Wittig successively discovered lithium–halogen exchange in aryl halides and directed ortho-lithiation of aromatic compounds by substituent heteroatoms. These reactions have become important methods for forming carbon–lithium bonds and constructing complex molecular structures.

subquestions.text_open:
8.2 Ortho-lithiation can be viewed as being controlled by two limiting mechanisms: a coordination mechanism and an acid–base mechanism. In most cases, both mechanisms influence the reaction to different extents. A schematic of the coordination mechanism is shown below.
8.2.1 TMEDA (tetramethylethylenediamine) and butyllithium can form a dinuclear complex with the formula $Li_2Bu_2(TMEDA)_2$, in which both Li atoms are 4-coordinate. Write its SMILES string.

text_images.description: Schematic of the coordination mechanism: substrate '[H]C1=C(C=CC=C1)CN([R])[R]' forms intermediate '[H]C1=C(C=CC=C1)C[N]([R])([R])[Li]CCCC' through a reversible arrow labeled nBuLi, and the intermediate gives product '[R][N]1([R])CC2=C(C=CC=C2)[Li]1' through a single arrow. A curved arrow runs from the nBu-Li bond to the ortho H atom of the benzene ring. In the product, Li and N are joined by a dashed coordination bond to form a five-membered chelate ring. R2 is the original placeholder in the figure for the two R substituents on N; Li coordination in the intermediate and product is shown by dashed lines.

8.3 Lithiation reactions are also prone to side reactions, making control of the reaction conditions especially important.
8.3.1 The following reaction did not give the expected major product. Instead, E, which has the same molecular formula as the expected product, was obtained in 70% yield. Write the SMILES string for E.

A box on the right labeled 'Expected product' gives the SMILES representation 'CC1=C(OC(N(CC)CC)=O)C([Li])=CC=C1'. The structure of E is not drawn and is shown only as E.
